newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN strategic concerns override Burma rights issues.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN strategic concerns override Burma rights issues.

text.p: Strategic concerns appear to have outweighed pressure over human rights in the Association of South East Asian Nations' (ASEAN) decision to make Burma, along with Cambodia and Laos, full members next month.

ASEAN had been getting considerable heat from the European Union and the United States, which imposed economic sanctions on Burma over its human rights record last month, to defer the membership issue.

The seven ASEAN members -- Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- decided last year to admit the three as a group at some point this year. Admitting them as a group kept Burma from being singled out.

On Saturday, at a special meeting of their foreign ministers, the group decided the induction of its last three members will take place at the annual ministerial meeting in Kuala Lumpur on July 24-25, an event that will celebrate ASEAN's 30th anniversary.
Burma was originally invited to join ASEAN when it was founded in 1967 as an anti-Communist bulwark at the height of the Vietnam War. Rangoon refused.
Burma, a nation of 45 million people, rich in natural resources, could have taken its place alongside the emerging tiger economies of Southeast Asia had it done so.
But Rangoon took a different path, the "Burmese Road to Socialism", under former strongman general Ne Win in the 1960s.
By the early 1970s, Burma had retreated so far into isolationism it even walked out of the Non-Aligned Movement, which the country had helped found.

"It's important to have them in before they relapse again in isolationism. Right now they are too dependent on China," said Jusuf Wanandi, chairman of the supervisory board of Indonesia's Centre for Strategic and International Studies.
That was underlined on Friday when official media in Rangoon reported Burma had signed a broad economic and trade agreement with China, a move coming soon after the U.S. sanctions.
China is one of Burma's closest allies and is said to be its biggest supplier of weapons.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas referred to the strategic importance of the new members on Saturday.
"I think we are also taking into account the overall and long-term consideration of peace and security and tranquility in our part of the world," Alatas told reporters.
"We are complete now. And we are in a better position in ASEAN to contribute to peace and stability in our own region as well as in the larger region of East Asia."
ASEAN officials have also expressed worries that if the situation in Burma deteriorated further it could spill over into their borders.
Southeast Asian nations, who were reluctant hosts to hundreds of thousands of Vietnamese refugees for years, do not want to see a similiar exodus from Burma, analysts said.
ASEAN also believes the only way to reform Burma's generals, promote democracy and free markets, is through "constructive engagement" with the regime from within the fold.

But Western diplomats say admitting Burma would strain ASEAN's vaunted unity through consensus, undermine the respect it has earned in the West and compound the problems the group faces in creating an ASEAN Free Trade Area.

The admission of the three new members has established a dual-track system in the evolving ASEAN Free Trade Area. Current members have until 2003 to dismantle tariffs, except for Vietnam which must do so by 2006. The new members have until 2008.

When she makes her first visit to the region next month, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright will be in the ticklish position of dealing with an ASEAN that now includes a military regime Washington finds odious.
The United States, along with other Western and Asian powers, will have a series of meetings with ASEAN member nations after the grouping's annual meeting.
But in what appears to be a concession to the West, Burma and the other new members would not be assigned "dialogue partners" this year, essentially sidelining them at the meetings.
